rubrics.evidence: In agent.patch, src/core/context.ts now holds only `private actionObserver: ActionObserver`, `valueObserver: ValueObserver`, `targetObserver: TargetObserver`, and `outletObserver: OutletObserver`, constructs them in the constructor, and `connect()`/`disconnect()` merely call `start()`/`stop()` on those collaborators. The inlined action/value/target/outlet maps, observer-delegate methods, and management methods are removed from Context. New dedicated files implement each wiring: action_observer.ts (ValueListObserverDelegate + binding registration), value_observer.ts (StringMapObserverDelegate + change callbacks), target_observer.ts (TokenListObserverDelegate + target callbacks), and outlet_observer.ts (AttributeObserverDelegate/SelectorObserverDelegate + outlet callbacks), with TargetObserver/OutletObserver forwarding lifecycle notifications via `this.context.invokeControllerMethod(...)`.
rubrics.criterion: In the per-controller runtime class (src/core/context.ts, class Context in the injected state), none of the four controller-side wirings is implemented on the coordination class itself anymore: action binding observation/registration, value-attribute observation and change propagation, target token observation, and outlet selector/attribute observation are each delegated to a dedicated single-purpose class that the coordination class composes, starts and stops, and receives target/outlet lifecycle notifications from.

rubrics.evidence: In the patched application.ts, Application implements only ErrorHandler and composes dedicated owners: `readonly dispatcher: Dispatcher` and `readonly router: Router`, constructed as `this.dispatcher = new Dispatcher(this)` and `this.router = new Router(this)`. start()/stop() boot them via `this.dispatcher.start()/stop()` and `this.router.start()/stop()`. Registry and dispatch duties are delegated: `this.router.loadDefinition`, `this.router.unloadIdentifier`, `this.router.controllers`, `this.router.getControllerForElementAndIdentifier`, `this.router.getContextForElementAndIdentifier`, `this.router.proposeToConnectScopeForElementAndIdentifier`, `this.router.modules`, and `this.router.contexts`. The inlined state and methods from the smell (scopeObserver, scopesByIdentifier, modulesByIdentifier, eventListenerMaps, eventListeningStarted, createScopeForElementAndIdentifier, scopeConnected/Disconnected, connectModule/disconnectModule, eventListeners, bindingConnected/bindingDisconnected, fetchEventListener*, cacheKey) are removed from Application and now live in the new Router and Dispatcher classes.
rubrics.criterion: In the application root class (src/core/application.ts, class Application in the injected state), neither the installation's scope/module registry duties (scope observation delegate, identifier-to-module and element-plus-identifier-to-scope/context bookkeeping, scope proposal/booking) nor the event-listener table and binding connect/disconnect dispatch protocol are maintained by the root class itself; both areas are delegated to dedicated classes that the root composes and boots.

rubrics.evidence: The repair reintroduces focused owners that hold their concern state as private fields: ActionObserver has `private observer?` and `private bindingsByAction`; ValueObserver has `private observer` and `private valueDescriptorMap`; TargetObserver has `private observer?` and `private readonly targetsByName`; OutletObserver has `private started`, `private readonly outletsByName`, `private readonly outletElementsByName`, `private selectorObserverMap`, `private attributeObserverMap`; Dispatcher has `private eventListenerMaps` and `private eventListeningStarted`; Router has `private scopeObserver`, `private scopesByIdentifier`, `private modulesByIdentifier`. The coordinators no longer carry that per-concern state: Application's fields are only `element`, `schema`, `actionDescriptorFilters`, `logger`, `debug`, `dispatcher`, and `router`, with all scope/module/listener maps removed; Context's fields are only `module`, `scope`, `controller`, and the four observer references, with the previous action/value/target/outlet maps and observers removed.
rubrics.criterion: The concern-owning classes introduced by the repair keep the state of their concern as their own private fields — the per-concern registries (action-to-binding map, value descriptor map and string-map observer, target element tables with their lazily created token observation, outlet controller/element tables, per-outlet selector and attribute observers, and started flags) and the listener tables — so the two coordination classes carry none of that per-concern state as their own fields.

rubrics.evidence: Application.start()/stop() delegate to concern owners: `this.dispatcher.start(); this.router.start();` and `this.dispatcher.stop(); this.router.stop();`, instead of inlining scope/event-listener sequencing. Context.connect() delegates to the four observers in order: `this.actionObserver.start(); this.valueObserver.start(); this.targetObserver.start(); this.outletObserver.start();`, and Context.disconnect() delegates in reverse: `this.outletObserver.stop(); this.targetObserver.stop(); this.valueObserver.stop(); this.actionObserver.stop();`. Context.refresh() delegates to `this.outletObserver.refresh()`. No absorbed observer begin/end sequencing is performed directly in the coordinators.
rubrics.criterion: The coordination classes' lifecycle methods order and delegate rather than inline: connect/disconnect on the per-controller class and start/stop on the root class hand lifecycle control to the concern owners (their start/stop-equivalent interfaces) instead of performing each absorbed observer group's begin/end sequencing directly.

rubrics.evidence: The agent patch does not modify src/core/outlet_properties.ts, so the production caller remains `controller.application.proposeToConnectScopeForElementAndIdentifier(element, outletName)` from the injected smell, invoking the root Application class directly. Although Application now delegates this method to `this.router.proposeToConnectScopeForElementAndIdentifier(...)`, the caller still reaches the root coordination class rather than the Router that owns scope-registry duty, which is exactly the broken boundary the rubric warns against.
rubrics.criterion: The outlet property blessing path that ensures an outlet controller's scope exists (the production caller in src/core/outlet_properties.ts that the injection rewired from a routing subordinate to the root class) now reaches whichever class owns the scope-registry duty after the repair, not the root coordination class.

rubrics.evidence: In the injected state, Application had `get dispatcher(): Application { return this }`, a self-referential alias. The agent's patch replaces this with `readonly dispatcher: Dispatcher` initialized as `this.dispatcher = new Dispatcher(this)` in the constructor, where the recreated `Dispatcher` class owns `eventListenerMaps` and `eventListeningStarted` and all binding/event-listener cache methods. Call sites now reach the real owner: `Context` exposes `get dispatcher() { return this.application.dispatcher }` and `ActionObserver` calls `this.context.dispatcher.bindingConnected(binding)` / `bindingDisconnected(...)`. No test or fixture modifications appear in the patch.
rubrics.criterion: The root class's `dispatcher` property — which in the injected state returns the root object itself — no longer self-substitutes: whatever still consumes it (including the listener-table inspection that the runtime's own tests perform through it) reaches the class that actually owns the event-listener state, either because the property exposes that owner or because the call sites were re-routed, and the consumption surface keeps working without modifying tests or fixtures.

rubrics.evidence: The new concern-owning classes route errors and lifecycle activity through the same sinks as before. ActionObserver forwards bindings via this.context.dispatcher.bindingConnected/Disconnected (the application's dispatcher). ValueObserver keeps the identical error path: it catches TypeError, rewrites the message using this.context.identifier, and rethrows (no swallowing). TargetObserver and OutletObserver fire callbacks through this.context.invokeControllerMethod, the same context-owned path the context previously used as delegate. Router still implements ErrorHandler with handleError forwarding to this.application.handleError, preserving the scope-observer delegate's single error path. Context still implements ErrorHandler (handleError→application) and logDebugActivity→application.logDebugActivity. No collaborator duplicates handleError, swallows, or logs through a divergent path.
rubrics.criterion: Errors and lifecycle debug activity raised inside the new concern-owning classes still propagate to the same sinks as before the repair: they are reported through the owning coordination class's single error path and lifecycle logging (the context's controller-scoped reporting and the application's error handler), instead of being duplicated per collaborator, swallowed, or logged through divergent paths.

rubrics.evidence: OutletObserver obtains application-level services through explicit interfaces rather than raw maps: it scans `this.context.application.modules` and `this.context.application.contexts` and resolves outlets via `this.context.application.getControllerForElementAndIdentifier(...)` (outlet_observer.ts). Application exposes these as deliberate getters/methods delegating to Router (`get modules() { return this.router.modules }`, `get contexts() { return this.router.contexts }`, `proposeToConnectScopeForElementAndIdentifier` calls `this.router...`). ActionObserver routes bindings through `this.context.dispatcher.bindingConnected/bindingDisconnected` instead of touching event-listener maps. No collaborator is handed `modulesByIdentifier`, `scopesByIdentifier`, or `eventListenerMaps`.
rubrics.criterion: The concern-owning classes obtain application-level services (creating or looking up contexts, modules and scopes for outlet resolution and dependency scanning) through the coordination classes' explicit interfaces, rather than each collaborator reaching into another object's internals or being handed raw map/table fields from it.

rubrics.evidence: The patch leaves unused forwarding members on Application that only exist to serve the absorbed Router responsibilities: `get controllerAttribute(): string { return this.schema.controllerAttribute }` and `getContextForElementAndIdentifier(element: Element, identifier: string): Context | undefined { return this.router.getContextForElementAndIdentifier(element, identifier) }`. The previous internal caller of `getContextForElementAndIdentifier` was rewritten to call `this.router.getControllerForElementAndIdentifier` directly, and no call site in the patch references `application.controllerAttribute`. These are exactly the “compatibility helpers with no callers” the rubric requires to be cleaned up.
rubrics.criterion: The consolidation's leftovers are fully cleaned up: no member, field, protocol implementation or type imported on the coordination classes survives only to serve the absorbed responsibilities (for example remnant observation-delegate methods with no remaining purpose, per-concern fields that are no longer read where they were moved from, or compatibility helpers with no callers), and no class left behind by the repair is dead, unused or exported without need.

rubrics.evidence: Application no longer implements ScopeObserverDelegate or owns the event-listener cache; it constructs `router = new Router(this)` and `dispatcher = new Dispatcher(this)` and delegates only a handful of members to them, with scope/module and binding/event-listener methods removed. Context instantiates four distinct single-purpose owners (`ActionObserver`, `ValueObserver`, `TargetObserver`, `OutletObserver`) and its connect/disconnect simply start/stop them, after removing the inline action/value/target/outlet maps and delegate methods. The coordinators are not left as wide facades with dozens of forwarders, and the four wirings are split rather than collapsed into one catch-all class.
rubrics.criterion: The coordination classes are not left as wide delegation facades: the repair is rejected if the per-controller or root class still exposes a large surface of one-line forwarding members (dozens of methods that exist only to re-expose operations that now live on the new owners) instead of the intended narrow coordinator role, or if the four controller wirings were moved into one new catch-all class rather than distinct single-purpose owners.

rubrics.evidence: In agent.patch src/core/context.ts, Context.connect() starts all wiring before invoking the controller connect callback: this.actionObserver.start(); this.valueObserver.start(); this.targetObserver.start(); this.outletObserver.start(); then try { this.controller.connect() }. ValueObserver.start() also calls invokeChangedCallbacksForDefaultValues() before connect. Context.disconnect() runs controller.disconnect() first in a try/catch, then tears down observers afterward: this.outletObserver.stop(); this.targetObserver.stop(); this.valueObserver.stop(); this.actionObserver.stop(). This preserves the required ordering: targets/outlets/values are active before connect and observer teardown occurs after disconnect callbacks, avoiding the listed regressions.
rubrics.criterion: Controller lifecycle ordering regresses: controller-instance connect must observe every wiring already active (targets/outlets connected, values defaulted) and disconnect must tear down after disconnect callbacks run; visible failure such as change or connected callbacks firing before the connect callback, targets/outlets not yet reported at connect time, or callbacks still firing after disconnect.

rubrics.evidence: In agent.patch src/core/value_observer.ts, ValueObserver invokes callbacks on the controller instance: `changedMethod.call(this.context.controller, value, oldValue)`, preserving the `${name}Changed` contract and current/previous value arguments. Default/absent-value invocation at connect is retained: `start()` calls `this.invokeChangedCallbacksForDefaultValues()`, which fires `this.invokeChangedCallback(name, writer(defaultValue), undefined)` when `defaultValue != undefined && !this.context.controller.data.has(key)`. `stringMapKeyAdded` also uses `this.context.controller` as receiver via `descriptor.writer((this.context.controller as any)[key])` and `descriptor.writer(descriptor.defaultValue)`. Context.connect calls `this.valueObserver.start()`, so the default-value walk still occurs during connect. The callbacks are not bound to the new ValueObserver receiver, and the signature/default invocation are unchanged.
rubrics.criterion: Value change callbacks regress: callbacks must be called on the controller instance (not on the wiring class) as receiver, resolved by the same key-name-based method contract, with the same arguments (current value and previous value) and default/absent-value invocation at connect; binding them to the new collaborator receiver, changing signature or omitting default invocation breaks user controllers.

rubrics.evidence: The patch restores a dedicated Dispatcher collaborator owning the listener table: `eventListenerMaps: Map<EventTarget, Map<string, EventListener>>`, with `fetchEventListener` reusing an existing entry keyed by `cacheKey(eventName, eventOptions)` (sorted option keys including capture), so equivalent bindings share one listener. `start()`/`stop()` connect/disconnect all cached listeners, and `createEventListener` connects immediately when `eventListeningStarted` is true. `bindingDisconnected` only clears the listener via `clearEventListenersForBinding` when `!eventListener.hasBindings()`, preventing detachment while bindings remain active. ActionObserver routes `bindingConnected`/`bindingDisconnected` to `this.context.dispatcher`, preserving the shared cache and remove-on-disconnect semantics.
rubrics.criterion: Event dispatch and listener-table semantics regress: listeners must stay cached per event target and event name (capture option included), shared across equivalent bindings, attached when event listening starts and removed for a binding when it disconnects; concrete failures are duplicated listener registrations for equivalent bindings, lost or duplicated events after targets are added/removed repeatedly, or listeners detached while bindings are still active.

rubrics.evidence: The agent restores a Router with proposeToConnectScopeForElementAndIdentifier that drives the scope observer (parseValueForElementAndIdentifier + elementMatchedValue), and Application.proposeToConnectScopeForElementAndIdentifier delegates to this.router, so the not-yet-connected provider auto-connect path used by outlet_properties.ts is preserved. OutletObserver retains the same lifecycle wiring: connectOutlet/disconnectOutlet call outletConnected/outletDisconnected, which invoke this.context.invokeControllerMethod(`${namespaceCamelize(name)}OutletConnected/Disconnected`, ...) so the defining controller remains the receiver. The cross-controller dependency walk is intact: OutletObserver.outletDependencies iterates this.context.application.modules and readInheritableStaticArrayValues(constructor,'outlets'), dependentContexts filters application.contexts by dependentControllerIdentifiers, and start() calls this.dependentContexts.forEach((context) => context.refresh()); Context.refresh delegates to this.outletObserver.refresh(), so provider appear/disappear still triggers dependent consumer refresh.
rubrics.criterion: Outlet resolution regresses: outlet getters against not-yet-connected provider controllers must still auto-connect them via the scope-proposal path, outlet connected/disconnected callbacks must fire with the defining controller as receiver via the same lifecycle wiring, and a provider controller appearing or disappearing must trigger dependent consumers' refresh (including the indirect cross-controller dependency walk the injected class performs).
